extracted.intended_audience: college mathematics instructors, curriculum designers, and mathematics-education researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing instruction that fosters mathematical understanding and problem-solving competence in college students, focusing on cognitive resources, control processes, and belief systems, plus classroom practices to operationalize these goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources (knowledge possessed by the individual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts and algorithms; relevant competencies, including the use of routine procedures, 'local' decision-making, and implementing 'local' heuristics; problem schemata; representations; domain-specific knowledge accessible in long-term memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should inventory and solidify students' domain-specific facts, procedures, schemata, and representations. The paper emphasizes that possession alone is insufficient — access and representation matter (e.g., experts perceive deep structure via schemata). Examples and citations (Simon, Chi et al., Silver) illustrate how differences in stored knowledge and its organization affect problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and representation of resources (seeing relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether knowledge that a student 'has' will be seen as relevant and thus called into play on a given problem; the role of representation and schemata in making resources accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching must address how knowledge is represented and how to evoke it (e.g., using appropriate representations and schema-evoking contexts). Failure modes include students who 'know' facts but do not 'see' their relevance; remedy via tasks that surface and connect representations to problem contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic fluency (knowledge and use of problem-solving strategies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluency in heuristic strategies (general problem-solving heuristics and their domain-specific implementations) as part of the resource set available to problem solvers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach heuristics explicitly (e.g., 'assume you have the object and determine its properties' / 'draw a figure to see what properties it has'), provide domain-specific instantiations, and practice application so heuristics become usable tools. The paper treats heuristics on par with facts and schemata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (selection and implementation of tactical resources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Planning, monitoring, assessment, decision-making, and conscious metacognitive acts that select and deploy cognitive resources during problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents failures caused by poor control (e.g., wild-goose chases, pursuing a single approach unchecked). Instruction should develop students' 'executive' behaviors: generate approaches, evaluate them, monitor progress, and terminate unproductive paths. Use transcripts and examples to show how lack of control dooms otherwise capable students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling and legitimizing control processes (teacher thinking aloud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the teacher's decision process explicit: pose options aloud, justify selecting an approach, and pause to assess progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because control processes are invisible to students, teachers should model them during real problem solving (e.g., 'What are the options? We might look at A, B, or C. It looks like A might be worth a try for a few minutes because...'). This legitimizes monitoring and assessment and provides students with a template to internalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive questions to guide control
rubrics_metrics.description: Three posted/explicit questions students should ask during problem solving: 'What (exactly) are you doing?'; 'Why are you doing it?'; 'How does it help you?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions routinely (e.g., poster in classroom, small-group work) to catalyze students' internalization of monitoring and assessment. The paper reports that inability to answer these signals wasted effort and helps students learn to be 'in control' of their processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom format: whole-class problem solving with teacher as manager
rubrics_metrics.description: The class works a problem as a whole while the teacher acts as an external 'manager' who elicits suggestions, ensures understanding, nominates representations, and orchestrates pauses to evaluate directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reasonably difficult problems (10–50 minutes) and keep teacher interventions minimal and managerial: check understanding, prompt representations, require justification, pause periodically to ask 'Is this working?'. After solutions, perform a 'post-mortem' discussing representations, control strategies used/unused, and salvageable elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom format: small-group problem solving with teacher as roving consultant
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide class into small groups (e.g., four) working problems while the teacher circulates, providing hints in the form of heuristic questions rather than direct solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher responses should encourage connections (e.g., 'Does this problem remind you of anything?') and help groups practice control decisions. Small-group work provokes discussion and forces students to evaluate and choose among multiple approaches, approximating internal decision processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-mortem analysis of solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: After problem resolution, the teacher leads a reflective discussion on representations used, relevant background knowledge, effective/ineffective control strategies, and alternative solution paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use post-mortems to highlight what was useful, what could be salvaged, and to expose implicit reasoning. Occasional deliberate 'wild-goose chase' exercises can be used as teachable moments to show consequences of poor control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing belief systems (student perspectives about mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' beliefs about mathematics, the environment, the topic, and themselves — often unconscious — that determine whether they will select and use resources (e.g., 'Formal mathematics has little or nothing to do with real thinking', 'Problems are always solved in less than ten minutes', 'Only geniuses can create mathematics').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction must uncover and replace inappropriate (anti-mathematical) perspectives with ones that support use of mathematics. Beliefs must be probed (e.g., via tasks that require using formal reasoning) and explicitly connected to problem-solving value, otherwise classroom knowledge remains unused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probing and remedying misconceptions (use of 'Why?' and contextual tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated 'Why?' questioning and problem contexts that force students to reveal underlying misconceptions or beliefs rather than merely demonstrating rote procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give students tasks where their tacit beliefs will surface (e.g., construction problems, asking 'Why does that work?') and spend time unpacking their answers to legitimize proof and reasoning. This may require remedial discussion but 'unlocks' dormant knowledge in long-term memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional goal triad: (a) resources, (b) control, (c) beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: To train students to think mathematically, instruction must (a) provide students with a solid collection of resources, (b) assist in developing effective control behaviors (planning, monitoring, assessing), and (c) develop perspectives (beliefs) that promote use of mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three instructional aims are interdependent; successful curricula should plan activities and classroom interactions that simultaneously build knowledge, practice managerial processes, and surface/reshape beliefs. Separate problem-solving courses can help but these goals are desirable across ordinary coursework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active-learning and resource-connecting practices (Nickerson-inspired list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedagogical strategies to facilitate understanding: 'Start where the student is; promote discovery; insist on active processing; use representations; use analogies and metaphors; simulate; explore the reasons for misconceptions and errors; teach evoking conditions for procedures; vary the context; make connections among concepts; relate classroom teaching to real-world problems; encourage acquisition of domain-specific knowledge; reinforce efforts to understand; provide a generally supportive atmosphere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt these practices to promote resource acquisition and accessibility. The paper endorses this list as a concise summary of actionable recommendations from the literature; use them when designing tasks, examples, and classroom interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing and leveraging productive struggle (time and group norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use challenging problems that may take substantial time (10–50 minutes) and encourage students to struggle productively, with norms that permit suggestions and critique without shutting down participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about time: pause periodically to assess progress rather than enforcing arbitrary abandonment. Maintain a teacher role that critiques options without discouraging input; occasional controlled failures can be instructive for demonstrating control-process consequences.
